**Surah Nuh (peace be upon him)**

Its purpose is to demonstrate the complete power of God to do what He warned of ("sa'ala" (p-423)) regarding the destruction of those who were warned and the replacement of them with better people, and the power to bring about the Day of Resurrection, whose warning has been long delayed, while they turn away from it, deny it, and are heedless of it. Naming it after Nuh (peace be upon him) is the clearest indication of this, for his command concerning the destruction of his people because of their denial of him is established and recorded in his story in [this surah -]. (In the name of God, to whom belongs all perfection of majesty and honour. The Most Gracious, who has encompassed all things with the outward bounties He has bestowed. The Most Merciful, who singled out His friends with the obligation of obedience [at the beginning -] and the completion of His favour at the end.)

* *

When "Sa'ala" concluded with the warning to the disbelievers, who were idol-worshippers, of the punishment of this world and the Hereafter, it was followed by the greatest punishment that occurred in this world, through the denial of the Messengers, in the story of Nuh (peace be upon him). His people were idol-worshippers, they mocked him, and they were more rebellious than the Quraysh, more brutish, stronger and more numerous. None of that benefited them when the affliction descended, the vengeance settled upon them and the punishment came to them. The surah begins with a warning, as a cause of fear of the consequences of denying him, and says, emphasising it because of their denial that the Messenger could be a human being, or placing them in the position of deniers since they acknowledged his prophethood while rejecting the prophethood of others despite equality in humanity: (p-424) ﴿Indeed, We﴾, meaning, by Our overwhelming and far-reaching greatness, ﴿sent Nuh﴾, who was the first Messenger to come after the people of Adam (peace be upon him) differed in the upright religion of their father, ﴿to his people﴾, meaning those who were at the height of strength to carry out what they attempted, while they were on the verge of answering him to what he called them to, and of honouring him because of the closeness of kinship and language between them. They were all the inhabitants of the earth among the children of Adam.

When the sender, the messenger and those to whom he was sent had become clear, and sending implied the meaning of saying, he began to explain it as a clarification of what he was sent with, and said: ﴿That warn﴾, meaning, give a severe and profound warning, ﴿your people﴾ against persisting in disbelief.

Since the intention was "to inform them of that" at some times, because a person must have times of occupation with himself, such as sleep, eating and other things, he used the preposition to lighten the burden on him and to be gentle with him (peace be upon him), and said: ﴿before there comes to them﴾, meaning, while they are in their wicked deeds, ﴿a painful punishment﴾.

[And -] Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When God, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to be patient with his people in His saying: ﴿So be patient with gracious patience﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 5] (p-425) and to overlook them nobly in His saying: ﴿So leave them to plunge and play﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 42], He followed this with the story of Nuh (peace be upon him) and the repeated call of him to his people to faith. He singled out from his account his condition in the long duration of reminding and calling, because it is the intended point in this place, as consolation for His Prophet (ﷺ), and so that he might take him as an example in patience, gentleness and supplication, as was said to him (ﷺ) in another place: ﴿So be patient as the steadfast of the Messengers were patient, and do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], ﴿So let not your soul expire in regret over them﴾ [Fatir: 8]. Indeed the supplication of Nuh (peace be upon him) with his people lasted longer than your period, and despite that, it increased them only in flight [﴿He said: My Lord, I have called my people night and day﴾ [Nuh: 5], ﴿but my call has increased them only in flight﴾ [Nuh: 6], ﴿And indeed, every time I called them that You might forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears, covered themselves with their garments, persisted and were arrogantly arrogant﴾ [Nuh: 7]. Then the verses of the surah continued on this method of renewing the report of his long struggle, peace be upon him, and the repetition of his supplication, but that only increased them in distance and in determination upon their disbelief, until God seized them, and answered regarding them the supplication of His Prophet [Nuh -] (peace be upon him): ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant﴾ [Nuh: 26]. That was because he had despaired of their success. And in this there followed the urging of our Prophet (ﷺ) to patience (p-426) with his people and bearing with them, as He stated explicitly in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Take what is forgiving, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], and as was said to him [before -] ﴿So be patient for the judgement of your Lord and do not be like the companion of the fish﴾ [al-Qalam: 48], and ﴿And We relate to you the news of the Messengers by which We strengthen your heart﴾ [Hud: 120]. [Ended -]

When he had informed of his mission and its content, with what he had made known of the corruption that prevailed over them, he resumed his speech as an explanation of his compliance: "He said" — that is, Nuh (peace be upon him): "O my people," thereby winning their affection by reminding them that he is one of them, one who is concerned with what concerns them.

Since it is the nature of human beings to deny what they do not know, except for those whom Allah protects and makes submissive to faith in the unseen, he emphasized his statement: "Indeed, I am to you a warner" — that is, one who exaggerates in warning — "clear" — that is, my matter is clear in itself, to the extent that, because of its great clarity, it has become as if it were a manifestation of what it contains, proclaiming this to the near and the far, the clever and the dull.

Since abandoning the disbelief from which he warned them would not benefit them unless they believed, and since faith cannot be sound (ṣiḥḥah) except together with the abandonment of all kinds of disbelief, the essence (sirr) of the warning is expressed in His words: ﴿Worship Allah﴾, that is, the Greatest King (al-Malik) to whom belongs all perfection, and this is by making your turning (tawajjuh) to Him sincere, for His self-sufficiency (ghinā) prevents Him from accepting worship in which there is any association (shirk). This is faith (īmān). ﴿And fear Him﴾, that is, make between yourselves and His wrath a barrier (wiqāyah) that protects you from His punishment, by refraining from everything He dislikes, so that you do not move a movement nor rest a rest except in obedience to Him. This is the action that protects from every evil.

Since there is no way to know what pleases the King, so that one may adhere to it, and what angers Him, so that one may avoid it, except from Him, and no access to that except through his intimates (khāṣṣah), and no intimate is like His Messenger, whom He entrusted with His secret, He said: ﴿And obey me﴾, that is, so that I may make known to you what your intellects fall short of, concerning the attributes of your Worshipped One, your religion, your worldly life [and your return (ma‘ād)], and guide you to the acquisition of good manners that direct you and the avoidance of doubts that ruin you. So in my obedience there is a judgment that pleases the King with regard to you. This is Islam (al-Islām). Thus this call has combined faith, Islam and action, and these are the three pillars (al-athāfī) upon which the causes of success revolve.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 4:**

Since a human being is a place of deficiency, and does not cease to commit sin, nothing benefits him except the abundance of generosity (*fana' al-karam*). He alluded to this, encouraging them and appealing to their compassion, so that they would not despair and perish, by saying, as the answer to the command: ﴿He will forgive you﴾, that is, out of His generosity, beneficence and kindness.

Since some sins are not necessarily forgiven, namely those committed after Islam (p-٤٢٨)[ he said]: ﴿some of your sins﴾, that is, what preceded faith of polytheism and disobedience, and what followed faith of minor sins, which God graciously promised to expiate through avoiding major sins. This is among what He, glorified is He, made binding upon His own holy self by a promise that cannot be changed. As for other than polytheism, it is subject to His will, glorified is He.

Since a human being, because of his predominant forgetfulness and preoccupation with hopes, turns away from death as one who doubts it, or rather as one who denies it, He reminded them, warning them out of kindness toward them, so that they would keep in mind that they are in His grip and would desist from what angers Him, glorified is He. He said, indicating that a long life in disobedience, even with a comfortable living, is nothing, and threatening that He is able to destroy at any moment: ﴿and He will defer you﴾, that is, a deferment that benefits you. Know that all matters have already been decreed and their regulation completed, because of the all-encompassing knowledge and power, so nothing is added to them or subtracted from them. This is so that one knows that sending (the messengers) only manifests what is within the being, and does not suppose that it reshapes the essences by changing what the decree has determined concerning obedience or disobedience. Thus He said: ﴿until a specified term﴾, that is, God named it and knew it before He created you, so nothing is added to it or subtracted from it. Therefore your death will occur at its customary time, dispersed; otherwise He would seize you all together with the punishment of total annihilation (*'adhab al-isti'sal*). This is among the knowledge of what would not happen, had it happened how it would have happened (p-٤٢٩). That is because He knew that if they obeyed Noah, peace be upon him, their death would be at its customary time, and otherwise they would perish in a single destruction, like that of one soul. He knew that they would not obey him, and that their death would come only through the punishment of total annihilation.

Since a human being is created inclined toward vain desires, he might say, out of obstinacy or otherwise: "Why does He not make us immortal?" He weaned him from that, emphasizing it because the context requires it: ﴿Indeed, the term of God﴾, [that is] the one to which all perfection belongs, so none can repel His command, ﴿when it comes, is not deferred﴾. Before its coming, supplication, acts of obedience and righteousness may occur, and their blessing in it (the life) prevents distractions and makes life pure. So hasten to faith before the term comes, for once it comes, you will not be able to make amends, and faith will not benefit you after witnessing.

Since whoever knows this with certainty, and knows that when it is unveiled to him at the death-rattle (*al-gharghara*), he loves to be deferred so that he may repent when there is no more deferment, he does good deeds fearing the loss of his time and the inevitability of His hatred. He alerted to this by His saying: ﴿if you only knew﴾, that is, if knowledge, or its renewal at some time, were in your natures, you would know the admonition of your Messenger ﷺ that God does what He wills, and that the term is inevitably coming, and you would act for salvation. But you act, in indulgence in desires, the way one who doubts death acts.

[p. 430] Since he (ﷺ) was the longest-lived of the prophets, and his counsel to his people had been long and his trials with them prolonged, al-Biqa'i draws attention to this through the words that follow, which begin a new clause (mustaʾnifan): ﴿He said﴾, calling out to the One who sent him, because he was certain that none near to him existed other than Him. He omitted the particle of address, as is the habit of those who are near, and said: ﴿My Lord﴾. Since custom holds that repetition must have some effect, even if slight, and since their defiance of this was something one might doubt could happen, he said it again for emphasis, to show his grief and burning distress over them in their persistence in obstinate denial. He was complaining of his condition to God Most High, seeking His help, and seeking to draw out attention to what his exertion of effort was doing to him. It also served as an admonition to whoever would relate this account to them, even though the One addressed, glory be to Him, knows the secret and what is more hidden: ﴿I have called﴾, that is, I have directed the call to God, glory be to Him and exalted is He, with wisdom and fine admonition, ﴿my people﴾, that is, those who are worthy of answering me because of their knowledge of me and their closeness to me, and among whom is the strength to make the effort for what they desire.

Since the calling had encompassed all times, he said: ﴿by night and by day﴾, thereby expressing constancy.

Since the opposite of what was intended resulted from that, he said: ﴿But my call only increased them in flight﴾, i.e., nothing of their states in which they had been, ﴿except flight﴾, i.e., distance from you, aversion, repulsion, hatred and turning away, to the point that they were like startled donkeys fleeing from a lion. (p-431) He attributed the increase to the call because it was its cause.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 7:

Since fleeing (*firar*) is a metaphor for rejecting his call, he followed it with what explains it. He said, emphasizing (*mu'akkidan*) because their turning away despite this long supplication is something that can hardly be believed: ﴿And indeed, whenever﴾ (repeated over the times and in succession of hours) ﴿I called them﴾ [Nuh: 8], meaning to turn toward You in faith and sincerity toward You.

Since their turning away from what would benefit them was more repugnant, he mentioned what results from answering with faith, and said: ﴿that You may forgive them﴾, meaning that they would believe, and You would wipe out what they had neglected of Your right, and they had gone to excess in transgressing the limits because of it, with a complete erasure, so that none of that remains as a trace or a mark, so that You would not punish them for it or reproach them. ﴿They put﴾, meaning in every call, and this indicates the extent of their feigned deafness, by expressing the whole for the part. So he said: ﴿their fingers﴾, out of aversion to him and contempt for the one calling, ﴿into their ears﴾, literally, so that they would not hear the call, indicating that "We do not want to hear that from you. If you insist on calling, we will not listen, since we have stopped up our ears." They indicated their extreme aversion to the call by what his words ﴿and they covered themselves with their garments﴾ express, meaning they made a covering for their heads with their clothes, as one who is seeking this and very eager for it does, until they combined what prevents hearing his words and seeing him, to display their aversion to him and to his speech. Such is the condition of advisers with those they advise constantly.

﴿And they persisted﴾, meaning they remained in their evil deeds with a persistence in which they were fully turned toward them. It is borrowed from the *ṣirr* of the donkey toward the wild ass herd (*'ānah*), when he flattens his ears and turns toward it, driving it away and biting it, and it is used for turning toward sins and clinging to them, because one does so with the utmost desire, as if the doer were a wild donkey whose lust has been stirred. ﴿And they were arrogant﴾, meaning they produced arrogance, seeking it and desiring it. He emphasized this with his words ﴿with arrogance﴾, to draw attention to the fact that their action contradicts wisdom, for it was something they should not have done. Therefore it is something hardly believable. These verses have clearly proclaimed, in more than one place, that they disobeyed Nuh, peace be upon him, and opposed him in a manner more repugnant than which there cannot be, outwardly by blocking their ears and eyes, and inwardly by persistence and arrogance, and they did not agree with him by word or deed. So may the curse of God be upon them, and upon those who say that they agreed with him by action, because he called them to forgiveness while they had covered their faces. Covering is the act of hiding (*ghafr*)...

[p. 433] ...and similar nonsense of the fables which, if the most foolish of the worshippers of stones heard it, they would mock its speaker, though none are more foolish than they. This speaker said that only as a distortion of the Book of God, similar to the distortion of the Batiniyya (the esoteric sect), whom the Community has unanimously declared to be unbelievers for that distortion. May the curse of God be upon whoever doubts the unbelief of one who distorts in this manner, or hesitates to curse him. They are the Ittihadiyya (the adherents of unity-with-God doctrine), who went out of the religion at the end of time, and among their leading figures are al-Hallaj, Ibn 'Arabi, and Ibn al-Farid. Following them in this kind of raving are the people most foolish in intellect:

﴿They are only like cattle; rather, they are further astray in the way﴾ [al-Furqan: 44]. The erudite Imam, Burhan al-Din Ibrahim ibn Abi Sharif al-Maqdisi al-Shafi'i, the reliable and expert scholar, informed me of this, on the authority of one of those who are fanatically partisan toward them in this age, and he is among the notables of the teachers in Cairo, that he said to him: "What led me to criticize Ibn al-Farid was that I saw the words of his *Ta'iyya* to be contradictory. At times one understands from them incarnation (*hulul*), and at other times union (*ittihad*). He, in my view, is above that. So I knew that these people have a technical terminology (*istilah*), and our relation to it is a relation of incompatibility. When they hear a grammarian say 'the subject is in the nominative,' they laugh at him. Had we understood their terminology, we would not have objected." This is the meaning of what was transmitted from him, and it is something no one of sound mind would approve. It resembles what al-Mas'udi reported at the beginning of *Muruj al-Dhahab*, on the authority of one of the Christians who was credited with intellect and knowledge in the time of Ahmad ibn [p. 434] Tulun. He was tested and found to be as described in knowledge. He was asked about the reason for his steadfastness in Christianity despite his knowledge, and he said: "The reason is its contradictions, though it has been adopted by arrogant kings, learned scholars of great erudition, and monks who turn away from the world yet manage it. So I knew that the gathering of these categories upon adhering to it, despite its contradictions, could only be due to a great matter that compelled them to it. So I adopted it." He said to him: "Go to the curse of God, for you have wasted every intellect you possess." By God, he spoke truly about the great matter that compelled them to it, which is the decree and the power that compelled each one of them to throw himself into the Fire of Hell by his own choice, indeed by his desire for it, and to fight whoever would prevent him from it. That is the clearest proof of the perfection of God's knowledge and power, and that He is One with no partner, and no one can repel His judgment. In this is the confirmation of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "You will surely follow the ways of those before you span by span and cubit by cubit," and they are the People of the Book. I have fully discussed this in my book *al-Qarid fi Takfir Ibn al-Farid* (The Cutting Sword Against the Unbelief of Ibn al-Farid), in which I explained their defects and exposed their disgrace. Likewise my books *Sawab al-Jawab li'l-Sa'il al-Murtab* and *Tadmir al-Mu'arid fi Takfir Ibn al-Farid*. I have left nothing of that [p. 435] of any ambiguity. And to God belongs all praise.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 8:

When he (Nuh) mentioned his supplication at all times despite their turning away, and this was discouraging and necessitated ceasing the supplication, even though supplication after it was found to be extremely remote from him, in establishing it together with being absorbed in it in all states, just as he was absorbed in all times, he expressed with the particle of delay (thumma) to indicate the distance between the states, so he said: ﴿Then﴾, and he emphasized, for the sake of what has passed, that the sheer readiness of their attention to his call after that hardly deserves to be believed, let alone their increasing in it, so he said: ﴿Indeed I have called them﴾, [that is] to faith and to renouncing Satan.

Since loud calling is one of the two kinds of supplication, he put it in the accusative as a verbal noun, so he said: ﴿openly﴾, meaning manifestly, with a booming voice, generalizing to their whole company, the important and the humble among them, and with sincerity in that and persistence in it, until my sight nearly grew weary from the intensity of speaking to them and turning towards them, not hiding from them nor waiting for them, but by surprise; and I repeated that to them until I brought out what they had of answer, and I did not stop even when they stopped up their ears and covered themselves with their garments.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 9:

Since public proclamation (al-jahr) may not spread or circulate among their gatherings, he said, pointing out that he had broadcast that, and emphasizing it to indicate the severity it contained: ﴿Then indeed I proclaimed to them openly﴾, meaning I made it manifest, publicized and made it widely known, so that they would know that it is the truth from their Lord (p-436), because I am not shy of it nor do I find it shameful. ﴿To them﴾, meaning I singled them out with it; there was no personal interest in it in any way, for I repeated it to them after the obligation had fallen away from me. Since public proclamation was mentioned first, because it is closer to avoiding suspicion, and secret (al-sirr) is more worthy of knowing hearts and closer to winning them over, he followed it with it, saying: ﴿And I spoke to them in private, a private speaking﴾, meaning I called each one of them individually, so that it would be more effective in getting him to answer the call, more worthy of accepting the counsel, and more indicative of sincerity. All of that I did only for the sake of their counsel, with no personal interest for me in it. Since a person's seeking to be alone, with no one present and not occupied with any distraction, is very difficult, and so one hardly believes it, he emphasized it, saying: ﴿a private speaking﴾. In order to indicate, through this emphasis, the emphasis of what came before it of the actions, and the evident state of his conduct and of this order, along with what he stated of his effort (ijtihad), that he proceeded in it according to the requirements of wisdom: he first called the people nearest to him and most familiar to him, then moved on to those after them until the call encompassed them all. This call was in secret, each one individually, so that they would know his counsel and none of them would take it as rebuke or reproach. He then proclaimed openly so that they would know that it was a refuge (malja') from God (p-437) for that, and that it was a firm resolution, such that if they fell short in responding to it they would be punished. When they persisted, he combined secret and open; when they continued in their rebellion and the harm lengthened, he complained. In accordance with this, the "thumma" here indicates the distance between ranks, not sequence in time. It is possible that it indicates sequence, because public proclamation is further from suspicion, and then the announcement after it is further in distance.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 10:

When He informed that he (Nuh, peace be upon him) had exerted himself in calling (his people) to a degree beyond which there is no more, leaving aside no time and no circumstance, there followed from this an explanation of what he said in his call, which was the means to all happiness through repelling harms and bringing about benefits. So he said, putting first the seeking of forgiveness through repentance from disbelief, so that they might become receptive to being adorned with the praiseworthy religious qualities after being cleansed of base morals: ﴿So I said﴾, that is, in my calling to them: ﴿"Ask your Lord for forgiveness"﴾, that is, seek from the One who is good to you, who originated you, who manages your affairs, that He erase your sins, both their essence and their traces, by turning back from worshipping other than Him to sincerity in His worship.

When he had mentioned that he appealed to them first by showing that their return was possible, lest they say, "We have gone too far in sins, so we will not be accepted," and had informed them that seeking forgiveness is the gate of entry into obedience to the Almighty, he confirmed that appeal by saying, giving the reason for the command and for its answer (in the sense of "He will forgive you"), emphasizing it because of their hesitation: ﴿Indeed He has always been﴾, that is, from eternity and to eternity, constantly and everlastingly, ﴿Oft-Forgiving﴾, that is, characterized by the attribute of (p-438) veiling (sins) for whoever returns to Him in the most eloquent and sublime manner; and when forgiveness takes place, all harms are repelled.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 11:

When he had established the matter of repentance and explained its acceptance, he placed it first out of concern for it, because it is the foundation upon which everything else is built, and because emptying oneself (al-takhalli, removal of vices) comes before adorning oneself (al-tahalli, acquiring virtues), and warding off corruptions comes before attaining benefits and advantages. He encouraged toward it by mentioning what results from it of increase in goodness beyond the basic acceptance. From seeking forgiveness (al-istighfar) there arises great effects and bounties: the bringing of delight, through that which is a likeness of Paradise, the Paradise from which the cause of expulsion was forgetfulness, because they (people) love most of all the immediate gains and quick advantages, especially that which gladdens souls and expands breasts by removing misery. So He said, answering the imperative verb: ﴿He will send the sky﴾, that is, the green canopy, or the clouds, or the rain, ﴿upon you﴾, that is, with rain and kinds of blessings, ﴿in abundance﴾, that is, in a state in which it is frequent in its circuits, repeated. And this form is one in which the masculine and the feminine are equal.

﴿And He will increase you﴾ is the more apparent reading, because the context calls for emphasis, expansiveness and abundance, ﴿with wealth and sons﴾. This implies that whoever persistently seeks forgiveness (istighfar), Allah will grant him what gladdens him and protect him from what harms him. ﴿And He will make for you﴾, meaning in both abodes, ﴿gardens﴾, meaning great orchards. The verb is repeated for emphasis and expansiveness, since the context calls for it, so He says: ﴿And He will make for you rivers﴾, singling you out with this over those who do not do this. Whoever keeps to istighfar, Allah will make for him a way out of every distress and a relief from every worry. It is related that ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, asked for rain but did not do more than seek forgiveness. When he came down from the prayer, it was said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful! We did not see you ask for rain?" He said: "I did seek rain through the majadih of the sky (the stars associated with rain) by which the rain is brought down." Then he recited this verse. Al-Qushayri said: Whoever has a need with Allah will not reach his goal except by putting istighfar first. He also said: The deeds of the people of Noah were the opposite of this. Whenever Noah increased in admonition and in the ways of goodness and kindness, they increased in disbelief and heedlessness.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 13:**

Since whoever hopes for a king acts in ways that please him, and whoever fears him avoids what angers him, he alerted them to this by pointing to the majesty that calls for reverence and to the beauty of doing good to creation. He explicitly addressed them with encouragement (tarhib, the promise) while subtly hinting at warning (tarhib, the threat). He then said, beginning a new sentence in answer to whoever among them asks, "Is there anything left of your speech?": ﴿What is [the matter] with you﴾, that is, what thing happens to ﴿you﴾ while you are in a state in which ﴿you do not hope﴾, that is, you are at some time in a condition in which you hope, ﴿for God﴾, that is, for the King to whom all command belongs, ﴿[any] dignity﴾, that is, a reward by which He would honor you, even if it is small, for its little is greater than the abundance of others. And you do not fear from Him any humiliation through punishment, by knowing that He must hold you to account after the Resurrection, rewarding the obedient and punishing the disobedient, as is the custom of everyone with those under his authority. So you should revere His messengers by believing them, so that you may believe and act. For whoever wants to honor someone and magnify him does so in order to reward him for that, since the recompense is of the same kind as the deed. This only happens through knowledge of God with respect to His majesty, His beauty, and His character. You excel only through knowledge of God, not through deeds. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) surpassed the people only through something that settled in his heart, for knowledge is what causes deeds to grow and words to become sound. Glorifying Him (glory be to Him) is valid only by not seeing any right of yours over Him, and not disputing His choice, and by magnifying His command and prohibition, by not opposing them with dry leniency, harsh strictness, or interpretations that imagine submission. And His judgment is magnified by not seeking any crookedness in it and not contesting it with reasoning, and it should not have any purpose or cause. Because what is sought is the attainment of deeds, which are apparent causes, He expressed it with hope so as to gladden them, informing them that their deeds are effective. In other verses He expressed it with desire [tanbīhan] to indicate that in reality there is no cause except the mercy of God, for the state of supplication leads to that.

[p. 440]

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 14:

When this was an allusion to proving the resurrection by what they know of themselves, he stated it plainly after having hinted at it. He said, bringing the particle of anticipation, *qad*, because it is its proper place: ﴿And indeed﴾, meaning, while the situation is that He has indeed done good to you again and again in ways no one other than Him can do. This indicates the perfection of His power. Then He did not cut off His favor from you, so He deserved that you believe (p-441) in Him, because ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ [al-Rahman: 60]. It is also a hope for the continuation of His favor and a fear of its cessation. For He ﴿has created you﴾, meaning, brought you into existence from non-existence, shaping you ﴿in stages﴾, meaning, in successive states: first as elements, then as compounds that nourish the animal, then as humours, then as drops of semen, then as a clinging clot, then as a lump of flesh, then as bones, flesh, sinews and blood, then as another, complete creation, speaking, male and female, tall and short, white and black, and in between, and other matters that indicate His power over everything that can be power-exercised. [And whoever -] is able to originate this has greater power to restore it. His wisdom is established, and that He did not create creation in vain, by what has become evident of this transformation into these wondrous forms, which no one else has any power over in any way. Yet people frolic in this world like the frolicking of donkeys, the oppressed dies in his state, and the oppressor reaches his desires. So He must restore them in order to separate them, thereby manifesting His wisdom, His justice, His honour and His bounty. If He left this, it would be a deficiency in His dominion. And whoever is able to do this is able to requite with reward and punishment, so He is worthy to be feared and hoped in.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 15:

Since this [matter is clear -], but they are a stubborn people, whom only the bright sun at midday turns back, he reminded them, after the reminder of what is within themselves, with what is greater than that of the signs of the horizons, and divided it into the upper and the lower. He began (p-442) with the souls, because they, despite their nobility, are the nearest object of observation for them, and he followed with the upper, because it comes next to them in nobility and clarity of signs. So he said, [indicating -] the power to resurrect and to recompense with reward and punishment: ﴿Have you not seen﴾, that is, O people.

Since reflection on the modes [of creation -] requires precision and attention to wonders and subtleties that certainly indicate that its Doer is not incapacitated by anything, and [he] said, rebuking them for their lack of reflection: ﴿how God created﴾, that is, He to whom belongs complete knowledge, perfect power and absolute greatness, ﴿seven heavens﴾, which are at the utmost height, breadth, firmness and adornment. That they are seven is known from the adornment within them.

Since matching opposites with one another is extremely difficult, and hardly anyone can achieve it in every respect, he said: ﴿in layers﴾, that is, matching one another, one above another, and each one enveloping the one next to it. ”Without any flaws in them“: complete matching is not achieved except in this way, by enveloping from every side.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 16:

Since the encompassing (al-muhit) cannot be reached inside except by encompassing knowledge and power, He said, indicating the perfection of His power and His control, expressing it with "making" (al-ja'l), which comes about through causing and making to be: ﴿And He made the moon﴾, i.e., the one you see, while it is in the lowest heaven. He began with it because of its nearness, the swiftness of its motion, and its crossing of all the zodiacal mansions (buruj) once every month, and its disappearance during the nights of concealment (layali al-sirar) and then its appearance, and that is more wondrous as an indication of power.

(p-443) Since the heavens are transparent, He said: ﴿therein﴾, i.e., in all the heavens, ﴿a light﴾, i.e., a shining, spreading light revealing visible things. One of its two faces gives light to the people of the earth, and the second to the people of the heavens. Since its light is derived from the light of the sun, He said: ﴿and He made﴾, magnifying it by repeating the verb, ﴿the sun﴾, i.e., in the fourth heaven, ﴿a lamp (siraj)﴾, i.e., a great light revealing the darkness of the night from the face of the earth, and it is in the fourth heaven. Ibn Mardawayh, 'Abd al-Razzaq and al-Tabari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, may Allah be pleased with them, that: "The sun and the moon, their faces are toward the heaven, and their backs toward the earth." Al-Hakim narrated from him the mention of the moon, and He, glorified is He, made them both a sign of the vision of His righteous servants of Him in Paradise, for He sees each one [kullan] from his place, being alone with Him, and likewise they will see Him, glorified is He, plainly and openly, as they saw Him in the world through faith, by contemplation and reflection.

When he had shown the perfection of His knowledge and the completeness of His power through the creation of man, and then through the creation of something greater than him, He repeated the proof through the creation of man, because man is the greatest of created things and the most indicative of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, but in a different manner, one that clarifies some of what He had alluded to [in the first] of the detail (p-444), explicitly mentioning the Resurrection. So He said, using *al-inbat* (causing to grow) metaphorically for *al-insha'* (bringing into being): ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King to whom all command belongs, ﴿has caused you to grow﴾, that is, by creating your father [Adam], upon him be peace, ﴿from the earth﴾, that is, just as crops grow. He expressed it this way as a reminder to us, since it was the creation of our father Adam, upon him be peace, and because it is more indicative of coming into being and origination from the earth. He also indicated that He made our nourishment from the earth from which He created us, and by that nourishment our growth comes about.

Since their denial of the Resurrection was, in effect, a denial of the original origination, He emphasized it with the verbal noun (*masdar*) and placed it in a form other than the verb by stripping it of additions, indicating its ease for Him, glorified and exalted be He, and its lightness for Him, even though it is an act of innovation, initiation and invention. So He said: ﴿growth﴾. Along with this, the verse is suitable for *al-ihtibak* (a rhetorical device of mutual omission, in which each of two parallel terms is left implicit where the other is mentioned): the mention of "anbata" (He caused to grow) first indicates the omission of its verbal noun the second time, and the mention of "nabat" (growth) the second time indicates the omission of its verb the first time, so that the sense becomes: He caused you to grow a growing, and so you grew a growth.

Since death too is a proof of the complete knowledge and power, though it is not like the proof of origination through initiating creation, and since it is accepted with no dispute, He mentioned it without emphasis by the verbal noun (maṣdar), and said, indicating resurrection and rising: ﴿Then He will return you﴾ gradually ﴿into it﴾, that is, into the earth, through death and burial, however long the terms may extend (p-445) ﴿and bring you forth﴾, that is, from it, through restoration. He emphasized with the verbal noun that follows from the verb, indicating the intensity of concern with it and the certainty of its occurrence, because of their denial of it, and so said: ﴿a bringing forth﴾, that is, a strange one, not like what you know. Rather, you will be in it at the utmost of what can be of the everlasting life, your spirits joined to your bodies in a joining after which neither of them will ever be separated from the other.

Since the sprouting of a thing from something does not make that thing subject to its own disposal, He indicated the perfection of His power by breaking that customary pattern for them, as a favour upon them. So He said, making the Noble Name apparent once again, to magnify the proofs, lest His power be restricted by what the Name is associated with, indicating the lower world after guiding them to the higher one and then the lower world again, because His signs, despite their manifest nature, have become obscure through the abundance of familiarity with them: ﴿Allah﴾, that is, the One who combines all majesty and generosity, ﴿has made for you﴾, that is, as a blessing upon you, showing concern for your affairs, ﴿the earth a spread-out expanse﴾, that is, [it is easy -] for you to move about on it and to traverse it, like the ease of moving about on a carpet. Then He gave the reason for that, saying:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 20:

﴿That you may go about therein﴾, i.e., going along [its vast expanses] — [renewing yourselves for that] — ﴿in roads﴾, i.e., clear paths, much traversed ﴿wide highways﴾, i.e., having breadth, so that you may reach the far-flung lands by land and by sea, and thus benefit from all the regions. He who was able to bring you into being and empowered you to act upon your origin [despite your weakness] is able to bring you forth from your graves [which have never ceased to be subject to His command and the place of His majesty and dominion].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 21:

When they had argued with him, peace be upon him, after this clarification, whose indication of the intended meaning is beyond doubt for one who has attained purity of certainty, they increased their disputation, attributed him to error, disobeyed him with the most abominable disobedience, and met him with the most reprehensible words and deeds, he passed over that, alluding to it by his saying, resuming: ﴿Noah said﴾, that is, after his gentleness toward them and his leniency with them, complaining of them: ﴿My Lord﴾, that is, O You who bestow favour upon me, who manage my affairs, and who take charge of all my matters.

Since the weak are the majority of people, such that when they gather they outnumber the strong heads who are distinguished by wealth and children, and they seemed to be the whole, he said, emphasizing because their disobedience to him after that is something whose occurrence is unlikely: ﴿Indeed, they﴾, that is, my people whom I called to You despite my patience with them for a thousand years less fifty years, ﴿have disobeyed me﴾, that is, in what I commanded them and called them to; they refused to answer my call, fled from me with the utmost flight, and opposed me with the most abominable opposition. ﴿And they followed﴾, that is, with the utmost of their effort, looking to the conjectured immediate benefit after abandoning what is certain both now and in the hereafter, ﴿one whose wealth and children increased him not﴾, that is, [of] their chiefs who were insolent with their wealth and deluded by their children; he explained them by his saying: ﴿whose wealth and children increased him not﴾, that is, not anything at all.

Since wealth belongs to a person and the child, and it was proper that he should thank God who gave it to him, so that it would be good for him in both abodes, and likewise the child, he said: ﴿his wealth﴾, that is, by its abundance, ﴿and his children﴾ likewise. The word (waladuhu) here is the collective noun in the reading with a vowel on the second letter (walduhu), and likewise in the reading of Ibn Kathir, the Basran readers, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i with the vowels damma and sukun, on the basis that it is a dialectal form of the singular, like al-huzn and al-huzun, and al-rushd and al-rushud; or it may be a plural in this form, like al-usud and al-usd. Abu 'Amr's choice of this reading in this word alone serves to indicate, through the plural of multitude built on the damma, which is the heaviest of the vowels, that although their number increased and their strength grew great, they add nothing to them ﴿except loss﴾, through distance from God and blindness to the clear path. For the expansion of provision for them in this world was a cause of their transgression, their insolence, and their following of their desires, until they disbelieved and led others astray, and they were overcome, so they became the cause of their own wretchedness and loss by their loss; and in their view it had increased them in exaltation. In the context there is evidence that they gained no distinction except through these.

Since the abundance of chiefs was a further strength added to their strength through worldly provision, and the sense of the passage was: "I commanded them to believe, and they refused, and they commanded them to disbelieve, and they submitted to them," he joined to it, explaining their multitude by the plural pronoun referring to "min" (those), conjoining it to "lam yazidhu" (did not increase him), which is singular in pronoun form, taking the wording as a whole for its meaning, since the expression gathers both the singular and the plural in the judgment, so that it is the most indicative of what is intended by it. He said: ﴿And they schemed﴾, that is, these chiefs, in turning people away from me. He emphasized the verb with the verbal noun, indicating its strength, so he said: ﴿a great scheme﴾. He added to its emphasis with a form that is the utmost in intensity, so he said: ﴿kubbaran﴾ (monstrous), for it is more emphatic than kubbar (with the lightened form), which is itself more emphatic than kabir (great). So none of them called anyone to follow me in that scheme. ﴿And they said﴾ [Nuh: 23], that is, to them, in the lowest (depths) of the scheme that had taken place among them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 23:

Since the supplication of the Messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, was worthy of acceptance (p-449) on account of their dignity, sweetness, eloquence, splendour, and clarity in success, they emphasised their words: ﴿Do not leave your gods﴾, meaning, do not abandon them in any state whatsoever, neither ugly nor good, and they attributed them to the people in order to make them feel responsible for them. Then they singled out (the gods) by name for additional urging and explicit clarity about the intended meaning, so they said, repeating the prohibition and the governing verb for emphasis: ﴿nor leave Wadd﴾. Perhaps they were in agreement with the Arabs that wadd means abundant love, so the context fitted them by name with his saying: ﴿Wadd﴾. They repeated the negation for emphasis, so they said: ﴿nor Suwa'﴾. They emphasised this emphasis and went to an extreme in it, so they said: ﴿nor Yaghuth﴾. When the emphasis reached its limit, and it was known that the intended meaning was the prohibition of each individual one, not of the group taken as a collective, they dropped the emphasis, so they said: ﴿Yaghuth and Ya'uq and Nasr﴾, left free of emphasis because his intention was known.

These were righteous men. When they died, the people grieved over them. Then Iblis adorned for them the making of their images, as an incitement to act upon their good ways. So they made images of them. When time passed, he adorned for them the worship of these images in order to obtain worldly benefits through their blessings. Then the righteous people were forgotten, and they were made into idols, gods besides Allah. The worship of these was the first worship of idols. So Allah, glorified and exalted, sent Noah, upon him be prayers and peace, to forbid that, until what occurred between him and his people, which is well known. Then Iblis brought these idols out after the Flood, and their evil reached the Arabs. Wadd belonged to the Banu Kalb at Dawmat al-Jandal; Suwa' belonged to Hudhayl; Yaghuth belonged to Madhhij; Ya'uq belonged to Murad; and Nasr belonged to Himyar, to the family of Dhu al-Kala'. It has also been said otherwise, and Allah knows best.

Al-Baghawi said: Suwa' belonged to Hudhayl, and Yaghuth belonged to Murad, then to the Banu Ghutayf at al-Jurf near Saba'; and Ya'uq belonged to Hamadan.

Abu Hayyan said: Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi said: "I saw Yaghuth, and it was made of lead. It was carried on a bare-backed camel. They travelled with it and did not provoke it until it was the one that knelt down. When it knelt, they dismounted and said: 'It has chosen the resting place for you.' They would then dismount around it and build a structure over it."

It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, concerning the cause of the evil of those idols reaching the Arabs, that the Flood buried them, then Satan dug them up for the polytheist Arabs. The Arabs also had other idols: al-Lat belonged to Thaqif; al-'Uzza belonged to Sulaym, Ghatafan and Jusham; Manat at Qudayd belonged to Hudhayl; and Isaf, Na'ila and Hubal belonged to the people of Makkah. Isaf was opposite the Black Stone, Na'ila was opposite the Yemeni Corner, and Hubal was inside the Ka'bah. End of quotation.

Al-Waqidi said: Wadd was in the form of a man; Suwa' was in the form of a woman; Yaghuth was in the form of a lion; Ya'uq was in the form of a horse; and Nasr was in the form of an eagle. End of quotation.

This is not contradicted by the claim that they were images of righteous people, because their depiction of them may have been derived from their meanings. Thus Wadd was perhaps the most complete of them in manliness, Suwa' was a woman complete in worship, Yaghuth was brave, Ya'uq was a strong swift runner, and Nasr was great and long-lived. And Allah the Most High knows best.

[p. 452]

When He mentioned their plotting and what they had displayed of their speech, He followed it with what the listener would expect regarding their affair, so He said: ﴿And they have led astray﴾, meaning the idols and their worshippers by this worship, ﴿many﴾ of [Your] servants whom You created upon the sound natural disposition (fitrah), from among the people of their own time and those who came after them, for they were the first to establish this evil custom, so its burden falls upon them and the burden of whoever acted upon it until the Day of Resurrection.

Since the implied sense was: ﴿So do not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾, He followed it with His saying, using the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, to generalize and to attach the judgment to the attribute: ﴿And do not increase the wrongdoers﴾, meaning those firmly rooted in the attribute that necessitates that the effects of one characterized by it be, like the effects of one walking in darkness, disordered in their occurrence, in some of the things that are among them, ﴿except in error﴾, meaning a sealing upon their minds and hearts, until they become blind to the truth and to all their corrupt and misguided aims that are firmly rooted in error, so that nothing of them occurs in any manner in which there is any rectitude.

This came after Allah, glorified and exalted, had informed him that none of them would believe except those who had already believed. The discussion of it, in any case, is like the discussion of the supplication of Musa and Harun, upon them both and upon Muhammad (ﷺ), the best of prayers and peace, in hardening the hearts of Pharaoh and his chiefs, lest they believe at a time when it would benefit them, as has passed in Surat Yunus, upon him be peace.

Ibn 'Arabi went to an extreme in departing from the religion. He said in his Fusus: this supplication is good with regard to them. He also said: error is more guiding than guidance, and the one who is astray is in a better state than the one who is guided, because the one who is astray is always close to the intended pole (al-qutb, the pivotal axis), revolving around it, whereas the one who is guided is the possessor of an extended path, so he moves away from the intended goal. He made clear that Allah, exalted is He, did not create any creature more foolish than one who follows him in this, and those who go his way in the error that no intelligent person would accept, namely the worshippers of idols, who have no greater foolishness nor anything like it. Upon them, therefore, is the utmost disgrace and curse.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 25:

When he had finished with their affair in their misguidance, and had supplicated to his Messenger (ﷺ), nothing remained but their destruction. Among the implications of the clear misguidance and the removal of the sight, as water is lost in milk, he said, explaining His response to Nuh's supplication and mentioning the aspect through which they were destroyed, and he emphasised with the negating "mā" in form, against the opposite of the meaning of the statement, because the disbelievers believed that deliverance and destruction are the habit of time: ﴿Because of﴾.

Since the disbeliever had erred three times, in believing in the idols (ṭāghūt), in denying his Lord, and in denying His Messenger (ﷺ), and that was sufficient to deserve being seized, He said: ﴿their sins﴾, gathering them with the sound plural (jam' al-salāma, the regular plural ending) according to the recitation of the majority. The recitation of Abu 'Amr with the broken plural (jam' al-taksīr, the irregular plural pattern) conveys that, in addition to these principal sins sufficient for seizure, they had sins beyond counting, which necessitates intensifying that seizure. It therefore indicates that one should guard against every sin.

Since what is painful is their drowning and not that it came from a specific source, He said, informing of what He did to them in this world: ﴿they were drowned﴾, that is, by the flood, building the verb to the passive for this purpose and to inform that it is extremely easy for the one Chooser, the One, the Subduer. So the water went over them, over all the earth, the plain and the mountain, and left none of them. The same applies to what follows from it and comes after it, His saying: ﴿then they were made to enter﴾, that is, by the compulsion of the Compeller, into the Hereafter, whose first stage is the barzakh (the intermediate realm), in which they are presented to the Fire morning and evening, ﴿fire﴾, that is, very great, the lightest of it being what occurs at its beginnings in the barzakh. Shaykh Wali al-Din al-Malawi said: They were punished in this world by drowning, and in the Hereafter by burning and by despair of mercy, and what punishment is more severe than that? Al-Dahhak said: In a single state they were drowned in the water on one side and burned in the water on another side, by the power of Allah, glorified and exalted. In this is an indication for the view of others regarding the punishment of the grave.

Since they had relied on their gods to help them against the seizure of Allah, the Exalted, He said, giving as a consequence of this drowning and entering the mercy, so that this would be more intense in the punishment, for a person, as al-Malawi said, when he is in punishment and hopes for escape, the matter is made easier for him, unlike when he despairs of escape, informing that their gods are powerless, for they did not avail them anything, as a rebuke to whoever worships the like of them: ﴿they did not find﴾, and He confirmed the matter concerning them by His saying: ﴿for themselves﴾, that is, when Allah caused His might to descend upon them and brought down His vengeance upon them.

Since all ranks are beneath His rank, the Exalted, and no one may encompass all that is beneath His rank, glorified is He, of levels, He said, affirming the preposition: (p-454) ﴿besides Allah﴾, that is, the Greatest King, before whose rank of greatness all ranks are diminished, and before whose might and majestic force they are humbled, ﴿helpers﴾ who would help them against the one who intended this for them, so that they could prevent what He did to them, or take retribution from Him on their behalf, by what the witness of existence testifies, which is the most just of witnesses: that what Allah, glorified and exalted, willed of their drowning was fulfilled without any of them escaping, despite their multitude and strength, because they were His enemies. And the deliverance of His Prophet Nuh, peace be upon him, and of those with him, may Allah's good pleasure and peace be upon them all, despite their weakness and fewness, left none of them behind, because they were His friends. So just as none of those whom He intended to deliver was destroyed, likewise none of the enemies escaped. Whoever says, out of crookedness, what the storytellers say, he too is astray in the worst error. So the curse of Allah be upon whoever says that Allah, the Exalted, was not their helper, despite these indications which are explicit that He was their enemy, and that their help was only to His Prophet Nuh, peace be upon him. Believing this, or any part of it, is manifest disbelief from which there is no escape in any way. The one who says this is Ibn 'Arabi, author of the Fusus (the Bezels of Wisdom), who did not intend by his composition anything but the demolition of the pure Shari'a. Ibn al-Farid also versified it in his Ta'iyya, which he named Nazm al-Suluk (The Ordering of the Path). So the curse of Allah be upon him and upon whoever follows him, or doubts his disbelief, or hesitates to curse him, after he set up the misguidance by which he kindled the lands and destroyed many of the servants.

"When He had completed the account of their drowning, and placed it first to give importance to the magnification of the Messenger (ﷺ) in answering his supplication, as a warning to the Arabs lest they expel their Messenger (ﷺ) and bring upon him the like of that, He connected to the statement of Nuh (peace be upon him) from its beginning his saying when Allah, exalted is He, informed him that they would be drowned and that none of them would believe except those who had already believed, after his trial with them had lasted so long that a man would bring his son to him and say to him: 'Beware of this man lest he lead you astray, for my father warned me against him.' The form of generality is never definitive in its individual instances, seeking the fulfilment of His promise and an explicit statement of His intent: ﴿And Nuh said﴾, and he dropped the particle as is the custom of those in the presence of the Lord, and said: ﴿My Lord, leave not﴾, meaning, do not leave in any way at all, even in the slightest degree, ﴿upon the earth﴾, meaning all of it, from its east to its west, its plains and its mountains and its valleys, ﴿any of the disbelievers﴾ (p-457), meaning those firmly established in disbelief, which was innate to them and in their nature, ﴿dayyaran﴾, meaning anyone who moves about in it. It is one of the words of generality used in general negation, so it is said: from 'al-dur' or 'al-dar', there is no active form (fi'al), for otherwise it would be 'dawwar'. It is also permissible, and it is closer, that this supplication was made when he boarded the ship and the drowning of them had begun, meaning by it generality, out of dislike that any of them should remain on a mountain peak or the like, not the very act of drowning; and that the meaning of what precedes it be the ruling of their drowning and the certainty of the decree concerning it, or the commencement of it."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 71, verse 27:

Since the Messengers, may blessings and peace be upon them, say and do only that which contains the benefit of the religion (maslahat al-din), he gave a reason for his supplication with his words and emphasized it, to show his certainty in the belief in what had been revealed to him regarding the content of the words of God Most High: ﴿That none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ [Hud: 36], even though that was outside the usual course. ﴿Indeed, You﴾, that is, O Lord, ﴿if You leave them﴾, that is, if You leave them in whatever state they may be, preserving them safe upon the earth in the condition they are in of disbelief, misguidance and leading others astray, even if that state is base, ﴿they will mislead Your servants﴾, that is, those who have believed in Me, and those who are born upon the pure natural disposition (fitrah).

(p-458) Since it is possible that a person may be harmful and yet a beneficial child may be born to him, he negated that with his words: ﴿Nor will they beget except a wicked, ungrateful one﴾, that is, if You decree their continuance in the world, ﴿except a fajir﴾, that is, one who has strayed far from everything to which one ought to hold fast. He was content with the basic form of the active participle (fajir) to indicate that whoever exceeds the limit, or begins something after it of persistence in error, that becomes his habit, so he exaggerates; therefore he said: ﴿kaffar﴾, that is, one who conceals to an extreme degree what must be made manifest of the signs of God, because your saying "O Lord" does not fail at all. The apparent meaning is that this statement is not made except through revelation, as in Surah Hud, peace be upon him, in the words of God Most High: ﴿That none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ [Hud: 36]. Accordingly, even the young children of these people will be punished for what God knows they would have done had they reached maturity, not for what they actually did, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning the children of disbelievers: "God knows best what they would have done."

Since all of this shows that he prayed against the enemies of God, he also prayed for His allies, beginning with himself, for he was the head of that community. So he said, dropping into the manner of the people of special nearness: "My Lord" (﴿رَبِّ﴾), meaning: O You who have done good to me by making me follow those who followed me and by keeping me away from those who kept away from me, for whoever has a nature stamped with something, it cannot be turned away from it.

And since the lofty station is too exalted for anyone to estimate it as it deserves, he said: "Forgive me" (﴿اغْفِرْ لِي﴾), meaning: for even if I am protected from sin, nothing will suffice me except Your forbearance, Your pardon (p-459) and Your mercy. And since by his humility he manifested the greatness of God, glorified and exalted is He, he arranged those for whom he prayed according to the most deserving to the least: so he said: "and for my parents" (﴿ولِوالِدَيَّ﴾), and they were both believers, and they were Lamk son of Mutawshalakh and Shamkha daughter of Anush. Abu Hayyan said: Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: Among Noah's ancestors between him and Adam, peace and blessings be upon them, there was no unbeliever father.

He repeated the preposition (al-jarr) for emphasis, saying: "and for whoever enters my house" (﴿ولِمَن دَخَلَ بَيْتِيَ﴾), because one who is bound to a person by kinship has a firm right, especially if he is sincere in his love, and therefore he said: "as a believer" (﴿مُؤْمِنًا﴾). And since he specified, he then generalized, and again repeated the preposition for emphasis, saying: "and for the believing men and the believing women" (﴿ولِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ والمُؤْمِناتِ﴾), meaning: those who are characterized by this description in every community until the end of time, [and] do not increase them in any state of affairs in anything except success.

Since the implied sense indicated by the ihtibak (the interlocking of complementary elements) is: "and do not honour the apostates," he followed it with his saying: "and do not increase the wrongdoers" (﴿ولا تَزِدِ الظّالِمِينَ﴾), meaning: those who are most persistent in wrongdoing in any state, "except in ruin" (﴿إلا تَبارًا﴾), meaning: except in destruction that annihilates, shatters their forms, cuts off their descendants, and lays waste their dwellings. Just as God, glorified and exalted, responded to him regarding the people of faith and disbelief among the people of that time, so He responds to him regarding the people of faith and the people of loss, with happiness for one and perdition for the other, in all ages, until they stand before the Mighty, the Compeller.

The verse contains ihtibak: the affirmation of a prayer that entails the honouring of believers first points to the omission of a prayer that implies the humiliation of disbelievers second; and the affirmation of a prayer for increased perdition second implies the omission of a prayer for increased success first. This latter, which explicitly mentions perdition, is what the opening with warning indicated. Thus the latter corresponds to the former in the clearest and most complete manner, in the best condition and the finest attainment. There is no power and no strength except with God, the Most High, the Mighty, and praise be to God in every state.
